articles.body:
Eighteen editions on, China’s biggest annual shopping festival is growing up. As the sales frenzy gives way to longer promotions and more cautious spending, brands and platforms are rethinking how to win over shoppers.

SHANGHAI: Three models in wool coats stand before a wall of glass bricks as a cinema camera rolls past.

Behind a partition, operators in headsets monitor a bank of screens.

Nearly 400,000 people are watching the livestream by Chinese fashion brand CHICJOC on online shopping platform Taobao.

One viewer asks to see the grey outerwear. Another wants to know what to pair with an oatmeal coat. In the corner of the screen, a coat is listed for 3,499.99 yuan (US$526).

For CHICJOC co-founder Wei Yujing, 36, the carefully choreographed livestream is a far cry from the frantic sales race that once defined Singles’ Day.

Back in 2017 or 2018, orders opened as Nov 11 began, she recalled, with Taobao ranking brands by sales for all to see.

“It felt like the Olympic Games, with every brand starting from the same line on that one day,” she told CNA. “All the brands were like racehorses.”

“I remember some shops crossed 10 million yuan within an hour, or within a day,” she said.

Launched in 2009 by Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, which operates Taobao, Singles’ Day has grown into the world’s biggest online shopping festival.

Known in China as “shuang shi yi”, or Double 11, the festival takes its name from Nov 11 (11/11), whose four ones symbolise singlehood.

But 18 editions on, the shopping bonanza looks markedly different. What was once a 24-hour sales frenzy has stretched into weeks-long promotions and new ways of courting increasingly cautious consumers.

The scale remains enormous. Sales across platforms reached 1.695 trillion yuan last year during the Oct 7 to Nov 11 promotional period, up 14.2 per cent year-on-year, according to data provider Syntun.

But that growth was roughly half the 26.6 per cent recorded in 2024.

FROM MAD DASH TO SLOW BURN

The midnight rush that once defined Singles’ Day has largely been left behind.

Alibaba began making the shift in 2021, moving the start of its presales to 8pm. By 2022, its main sales windows were also opening at that hour.

The platform has also simplified its discounts, replacing complex cross-store coupons - such as spending 300 yuan to save 50 yuan across multiple shops - with straightforward discounts of 15 per cent.

Rival e-commerce giant JD.com scrapped its presale model in 2023 - shoppers previously paid deposits weeks in advance and settled the balance when sales opened; it now sells goods in stock outright.

The changes are a deliberate move away from the artificial urgency of the midnight launch, said Jason Yu, managing director at Beijing-based CTR Market Research.

“Now it all has moved to 8 o’clock in the evening so that everybody is all relaxed (and) sitting on the sofa.”

The platforms had been criticised over the pressure and complicated promotional rules, Yu noted.

“Now they want to create a more hassle-free and easy environment for consumers.”

The shift extends to livestream selling, where aggressive pitches are also losing their appeal.

“Early livestreams were mostly hard-sell, hawking-style selling. Someone in the livestream room shouts, ‘3, 2, 1! Last batch, 9.9 yuan with free shipping, if you don’t buy today it’s gone tomorrow!’” Liu Manting, a brand marketing manager at Taobao Fashion, the platform’s apparel business unit, told CNA.

“Consumers are actually really tired of that.”

For Zhang Ya, a 29-year-old pottery teacher in Shanghai, the appeal of chasing discounts has faded.

“The coupons in recent years have become too complicated,” she told CNA.

“Then you buy and stockpile a whole pile of stuff that takes ages to use up ... You might as well buy things whenever you need them. The price isn’t really that different anyway.”

“There’s no real atmosphere now,” Zhang said, recalling the televised Tmall gala that once accompanied Singles’ Day. Tmall is Alibaba’s business-to-consumer marketplace and sister platform to Taobao.

“People’s enthusiasm has faded a bit compared with before.”

Her preparation this year is limited to topping up a membership that makes returns easier.

But not everyone has lost interest.

Cao, a 22-year-old intern hoping to snag a discount on a computer, still finds the deals “pretty worthwhile”.

The shopping calendar has also stretched considerably, with campaigns now opening shortly after China's National Day holiday in early October and running for more than a month.

Alibaba and Douyin opened their campaigns on Oct 15, almost a month before Nov 11. JD.com launched its campaign on Oct 12, while short video platform Kuaishou and lifestyle app Xiaohongshu kicked theirs off on Oct 7 and Oct 10 respectively.

CTR’s Yu described the increasingly extended campaigns as an “arms race amongst all the different platforms”.

Fang Jun, 34, a Shanghai livestreamer who goes by Junjun on camera, has watched the single-day sales spike flatten out over the past six years.

“It used to be a big spike, with purchases concentrated on Double 11 and Double 12,” she told CNA, referring to another shopping event on Dec 12.

“Now it’s more like a small bump, a bit higher than usual but not by much.”

Yet even a smaller bump can pay off for merchants.

On a normal day, her company might spend 1 million yuan on advertising to make 2 million in sales, Fang said.

During the big promotions, free traffic from the platforms can cut that spend to about 300,000 yuan.

SPENDING WITH RESERVATIONS

Fang has seen the shift towards more cautious spending from both sides of the camera.

Before becoming a livestreamer, she worked in tourism and owned more than 20 luxury handbags.

“In the past year or two I haven’t bought a single designer bag,” she said.

“Back then people were conscious of money, but it was about how to live better,” she said.

“Now even people I know who earn tens of millions of yuan can’t bring themselves to spend. A lot of people around me now say: ‘Spend on what you must, and don’t spend a cent on anything else.’”

Consumers coming on to the livestreams have moved the same way too, she said. A few years ago, her company’s 300-yuan gift sets sold briskly.

But during this year’s mid-year shopping festival, known as 618, they struggled to find buyers.

“Items at 90-something yuan or less, even 40 or 50 yuan, sold very well instead,” she said.

Chinese shoppers are “becoming more cautious and pragmatic”, said CTR’s Yu.

“They look … more for substance and the real value that (they) extract from purchases,” he said, attributing the shift partly to pressure on household finances.

Shopping habits are also changing.

Rather than stocking up during major sales events, consumers are increasingly buying smaller quantities as needed, aided by instant retail services that can deliver orders within the hour, Yu added.

Some spending is also shifting away from physical goods towards experiences such as travel, concerts, football and outdoor activities.

Meanwhile, government subsidies continue to support purchases of big-ticket items.

In late September, China’s state planner, the National Development and Reform Commission, said it had released the fourth and final 62.5 billion yuan tranche of this year’s 250 billion yuan consumer trade-in subsidy programme, which covers products including home appliances and computers.

The programme has become part of the Singles' Day shopping landscape, Yu noted.

Home appliances were the largest product category at last year’s Singles’ Day campaign, accounting for 266.8 billion yuan in sales, according to Syntun.

But the search for value is not simply about spending less - it is also changing what consumers are willing to pay for.

At one end sits “dupe” culture - the hunt for cheaper alternatives to branded products.

Taobao is catering to such shoppers by connecting them with factory-direct sellers and merchants from industrial clusters, said Liu from Taobao Fashion.

At the other end of the market are brands such as CHICJOC.

Its customers are willing to pay a premium for products they believe will last, said co-founder Wei.

The brand does not offer discounts and raises prices on some of its classic pieces each year, much like luxury brands.

“And customers accept it,” she said.

Wei said her customers viewed a coat as an investment they could wear for a decade, and paid close attention to prices.

“If we adjust any price even slightly, they’ll find out ... Our customers even know our prices and the tiny differences better than our staff do.”

BEYOND THE BARGAIN

For platforms and brands, winning over China's increasingly selective shoppers now requires more than offering the biggest discounts.

At a sprawling studio about an hour’s drive from central Shanghai, Taobao is experimenting with a different approach to livestream selling.

CHICJOC’s fashion showcase is part of the platform’s Super Live initiative, which stages professionally produced shows to highlight brands and their products.

According to Alibaba, the format swaps the standard phone setup for cinematic cameras and couture-level runway production, weaves backstage design stories into the stream, and runs on a “see-now-buy-now” model - viewers can order what is on the catwalk as it appears.

Taobao has staged more than 100 such runway shows over the past three years, with every participating brand achieving its highest-ever single-day sales on the day of its show, said Liu from Taobao Fashion.

The strategy is also shifting purchases away from Nov 11 itself towards brands’ own promotional events.

CHICJOC’s VIP customers, for instance, tend to shop around the brand’s livestream events rather than wait for Singles’ Day, Liu said.

The brand’s two-day event in late October generated more than 61 million yuan in store sales, a peak so far this year, according to the company. Orders for one alpaca coat alone exceeded 10 million yuan.

Jacob Cooke, CEO of China-based e-commerce firm WPIC Marketing + Technologies, said Singles’ Day has moved away from being a “clearance event” towards engaging customers and launching new products.

For prestige brands, heavy discounts on signature products “can hurt brand equity”, he said, adding that using the festival’s traffic to launch something new is the smarter play.

Technology is also changing how shoppers discover and buy products.

This is the first Singles' Day where shoppers can use an artificial intelligence chatbot to search for and compare products, place orders, track deliveries and handle after-sales requests, without navigating the usual shopping pages.

In May, Alibaba connected its Qwen AI model to its catalogue of more than 4 billion products. Rivals JD.com and Douyin have also folded in their own assistants, Dongdong and Doubao.

Internal data from WPIC Marketing + Technologies for October shows AI already driving roughly 5 per cent of purchases through links embedded in chatbots.

AI has reached the livestream floor too. Some merchants on Taobao now use virtual hosts for overnight sessions, Liu from Taobao Fashion said, although they remain “more of a supporting tool”.

In apparel, she said, “people still mainly want to see how clothes look on a real person”.

The human faces behind livestreams are changing as well.

Brands are moving away from relying heavily on influencers towards regular livestreams hosted by their own employees within stores, where shoppers can browse products and make purchases at their own pace, said CTR’s Yu.

While the biggest influencers still generate “phenomenal” sales figures, their sway has waned considerably compared with previous years, he said.

For Shanghai livestreamer Fang, keeping viewers engaged now takes more than an aggressive sales pitch.

On a recent evening, she demonstrated a skincare product on camera, dabbing serum onto her cheek as she told viewers that the day's promotional bundle would disappear once the broadcast ended.

Pushing too hard risks putting shoppers off, she said. Instead, Fang tries to build rapport, greeting returning viewers with a casual “Hey sis, you're here!” before turning to the products.

“Good hosts sell themselves first,” she said. “If they haven't watched you yet, how would they even know about your product?”

While the frenetic pace of Singles’ Day has slowed somewhat, Cooke from WPIC Marketing + Technologies cautioned against concluding that the shopping extravaganza is in decline.

While the frenetic pace of Singles’ Day has slowed somewhat, Cooke from WPIC Marketing +

Technologies cautioned against concluding that the shopping extravaganza is in decline.

“More modest growth rates should be read as normal as China’s consumer market matures,” he said, noting that even single-digit growth is celebrated during Black Friday, the major annual shopping event in the United States that follows Thanksgiving.

He maintained that Singles' Day remains a useful barometer of consumer confidence, with continued spending growth pointing to shoppers who are cautious but resilient.

Olivia Plotnick, founder of Shanghai-based social media marketing agency Wai Social, was less convinced.

“I would not treat Double 11 as a meaningful barometer of Chinese consumer confidence,” she said.

“With the promotion period still being extended, year-on-year comparisons are hard to make.”

Fang, meanwhile, will continue spending four to five hours a day in front of the camera, persuading viewers that today’s offer is worth taking.

Despite the changes, the festival still holds a special place in her working calendar.

Asked what Singles’ Day feels like to her these days, she had a simple answer.

“Like Chinese New Year.”

The bustle, the anticipation, the biggest payday of the year. Hers falls in November.

articles.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
articles.preview: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday. Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
articles.body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.

Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

'Market purgatory'

The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.

"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.

"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

- Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

- Published6 hours ago

- Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

- Published3 hours ago

Strong jobs figures could ease market fears

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title: Ueno Bank scandal plunges Paraguay into political crisis
articles.summary: Suspected financial fraud, public money at risk and millions of customers affected: Paraguay is in serious crisis following the sudden collapse of Ueno Bank. President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment.
articles.preview: November 6, 2026 Suspected financial fraud, public money at risk and millions of customers affected: Paraguay is in serious crisis following the sudden collapse of Ueno Bank. President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment. The Ueno Bank collapse is turning into one of the biggest financial and political scandals in the history of Paraguay. At issue are suspected banking irregularities, hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, and business ties between the bank and the country's president, Santiago Pena.
articles.body:
November 6, 2026

Suspected financial fraud, public money at risk and millions of customers affected: Paraguay is in serious crisis following the sudden collapse of Ueno Bank. President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment.

The Ueno Bank collapse is turning into one of the biggest financial and political scandals in the history of Paraguay. At issue are suspected banking irregularities, hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, and business ties between the bank and the country's president, Santiago Pena.

The crisis was triggered on November 3, when the Paraguayan central bank (BCP) initiated resolution procedures against Ueno after determining that it had breached minimum solvency requirements. The public prosecutor has since announced three investigations into suspected financial crimes. 27 individuals have already been formally charged.

Pressure on President Pena intensified. On November 5, he tendered his resignation, but the Paraguayan Congress did not accept it. Instead, the Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to impeach him. A joint session of both legislative chambers was called to consider the resignation, but the session was not quorate, so no decision could be taken. Pena remains in office for now, and the Senate has opened impeachment proceedings.

What is Ueno Bank, and what happened?

Ueno Bank is a Paraguayan digital bank belonging to the Grupo Vazquez, a big Paraguayan conglomerate. Launched in 2021, it expanded remarkably fast: It recently had around three million customers, almost half the population of Paraguay. At the same time, there were warnings that the bank might have extended excessive loans to companies associated with its owners.

On November 3, 2026, the Paraguayan Central Bank (BCP) intervened, having determined that the bank had breached minimum solvency requirements: It no longer had sufficient capital to provide security for risks it had incurred. Business operations were abruptly suspended, leaving millions of customers unable to access their accounts.

What caused the crisis?

Investigations are primarily focused on three potential problems.

First, Ueno Bank is believed to have extended credit to other companies from the same group, and these may have exceeded legal limits.

Some business dealings may also have served to conceal the lack of capital, and make the bank's financial situation appear better than it actually was.

There is also the question of why the Central Bank didn't intervene sooner, despite indications that there were problems.

How much public money is managed by Ueno Bank?

Ueno Bank held huge deposits of public money. Its most important investors include the Instituto de Prevision Social (IPS), the Paraguayan social security agency responsible for pensions and social welfare payments. According to media reports, Ueno Bank administers public funds totalling as much as 800 to 850 million US dollars.

Not only is the size of the amount problematic, so is the concentration of public funds in a single financial institution — one that has had to be placed under state control. Other state institutions are also said to have continued to deposit funds with the bank.

This raises questions about how state institutions make their investment decisions, and the risks to which they have exposed public funds.

What are the bank's connections to Santiago Pena?

There is Pena's business relationship with Grupo Vazquez, to which the Ueno Bank belongs. The Paraguayan president maintained business connections with the conglomerate until March 2025, long after his election as head of state. However, he denies having had any direct involvement with the bank.

On the other hand, Pena's appointment of Carlos Carvallo as president of the Central Bank in 2023 has come under scrutiny. The decision is controversial because until then Carvallo was the chair of the finance company that became Ueno Bank, Financiero Ueno. It raises questions about possible conflict of interest, and the independence of banking supervision.

Carvallo resigned on November 3, at Pena's request.

Who else is under suspicion?

On November 4, the public prosecutor's office formally charged 27 people: eight Ueno Bank executives, and 19 others with connections to companies associated with the bank.

The investigations are looking into suspected breach of trust, attempted fraud, breach of duty in crisis situations, and violation of the legal obligation to keep records.

On November 5, a judge remanded several former bank executives in custody, including Federico Miguel Vazquez Villasanti, the president of Grupo Vazquez. Two other accused were placed under house arrest.

What will happen now?

The Central Bank has initiated winding-up proceedings against Ueno Bank. Deposits of sums up to the equivalent of 37,600 US dollars per customer are protected by law. A law has also been passed that will enable around 20,000 US dollars per saver to be paid out early. However, it is still not clear when the affected customers will actually get their money back, or what will happen to deposits greater than the legally protected maximum.

The political situation is more complicated. Santiago Pena tendered his resignation, but remains in office. A joint session of the two chambers of Congress could not decide whether or not to accept his resignation as the meeting was not quorate. The Senate has now initiated impeachment proceedings on charges of serious breaches of duty. Pena has announced that he will face the proceedings and exercise his right to defend himself.

What is at stake here is political immunity. If Pena leaves office in a regular way – by resigning — he will automatically become a senator for life, and this will give him parliamentary immunity from prosecution. If he is impeached, he loses this status, and can be prosecuted.

Should Pena leave office, the constitution decrees that his vice-president, Pedro Alliana, would take over as president. Congress would then have to elect a new vice-president. The current term of office runs until August 2028.

articles.title: Israel closes Hebron’s Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for Jewish holiday
articles.summary: Contested West Bank holy site is reopened exclusively for Israelis, deepening tensions over control of the mosque.
articles.preview: Ibrahimi Mosque reopened exclusively for Israelis, deepening tensions over control of contested West Bank holy site. Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron to Palestinian worshippers as thousands of Israeli settlers converge on the site for a Jewish religious celebration. The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and mosque employees had been barred from entering and the call to prayer suspended.
articles.body:
Ibrahimi Mosque reopened exclusively for Israelis, deepening tensions over control of contested West Bank holy site.

Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron to Palestinian worshippers as thousands of Israeli settlers converge on the site for a Jewish religious celebration.

The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and mosque employees had been barred from entering and the call to prayer suspended.

Mosque director Moataz Abu Sneineh told Al Jazeera that Israeli authorities intended to open the mosque’s prayer halls and courtyards exclusively to Israelis.

The closure, imposed on Friday afternoon and set to last until 10pm on Saturday, coincides with an annual Jewish observance to commemorate Sarah, a wife of Prophet Abraham, who is traditionally believed to be buried at the site.

Israeli troops tightened checkpoints and restricted movement across Hebron’s Old City, where the mosque is located, preventing some residents from entering or leaving their homes.

Israeli forces told The Jerusalem Post they expected about 20,000 visitors at the site for the Jewish holiday, with hundreds of security personnel deployed.

Israel’s encroaching control

The Ibrahimi Mosque, known to Jews as the Cave of the Patriarchs, is revered by Muslims and Jews as the burial site of the Prophet Abraham and members of his family.

Under a 1997 Hebron Agreement signed between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, Israel assumed security control over the Old City, while Hebron’s Palestinian municipality holds planning and construction powers.

However, in June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced a takeover of those powers, undermining Palestinian oversight of the holy site and raising fears that Israel was seeking to seize the site for exclusive Jewish use.

The closure comes just days after Israeli forces ended a 10-day siege of Hebron, which saw hundreds of arrests, 15 home demolitions and the displacement of more than 3,300 Palestinians.

Israeli settlers have steadily expanded their presence in Hebron’s Old City, seizing Palestinian properties and establishing new outposts under Israeli military protection.

articles.title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.
articles.preview: Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race. Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump. But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010. No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
articles.body:
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.

Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.

Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.

On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.

- Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

- Published4 hours ago

- What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

- Published2 days ago

2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure

Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.

That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.

Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.

Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.

In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.

"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.

3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future

Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.

Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.

El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.

His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.

This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.

Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.

Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.

- Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

- Published8 hours ago

4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned

Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.

Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.

Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".

That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.

"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.

"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.

"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.body:
Per il 5 novembre il Centro funzionale della Sardegna aveva emesso un’allerta rossa: si temeva il peggio perché temporali molto intensi e persistenti avrebbero potuto provocare piene importanti nei corsi d’acqua della parte orientale dell’isola. Fortunatamente le condizioni meteorologiche sono state leggermente diverse da quelle previste, quanto basta per evitare il peggio.

Lo scirocco, che avrebbe dovuto spingere i temporali verso l’interno, è stato più debole di quanto ipotizzato e i violenti nubifragi, che comunque ci sono stati, si sono scaricati prevalentemente in mare, a pochi chilometri dalla costa. È un esempio di incertezza previsionale in cui anche piccoli scarti possono produrre conseguenze molto diverse.

Qualcuno, non vedendo arrivare la pioggia, avrà forse pensato che le previsioni fossero sbagliate. In realtà, allargando lo sguardo, l’evoluzione meteorologica è stata sostanzialmente quella descritta dai modelli, ma con un piccolo errore di localizzazione. Un’allerta rossa non significa che ci sarà necessariamente un evento catastrofico, ma segnala il rischio di una situazione molto critica, per la quale è necessario adottare le misure di prevenzione contenute nei piani della Protezione civile.

Nel fine settimana e nei prossimi giorni sono attese altre piogge, visto che le correnti atlantiche entreranno più decisamente nel Mediterraneo portando anche un deciso rialzo termico. articles.summary: Partial results for South Africa's local elections were released on Friday, and showed the ruling African National Congress was headed for its worst-ever election performance with 32% of the votes after 80% had been counted.
articles.preview: South Africa South Africa's once-dominant African National Congress (ANC) was headed for its worst-ever election performance Friday with about a third of support after 80% of the votes from local government polls had been counted. articles.body:
South Africa

South Africa's once-dominant African National Congress (ANC) was headed for its worst-ever election performance Friday with about a third of support after 80% of the votes from local government polls had been counted.

Wednesday's municipal elections were dominated by concerns over failing water and power supplies in one of Africa's wealthiest nations which became a democracy in 1994 when the ANC took power.

With final results expected by Sunday, the election authority dashboard showed the ANC was still the largest party with nearly 32% of votes after 80% had been counted.

This was its lowest score yet for the ANC after it secured just over 40% at the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

At the heart of South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle, the party of jailed liberation hero-turned-president Nelson Mandela took nearly 70% of the national vote in 2004.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told AFP. "It's the ANC's worst result in history."

"It will undermine its ability to exert authority across South Africa, not just at a local level, but frankly at a national level as well," he told AFP.

"And opposition parties will be smelling blood when it comes to the next election in 2029."

The result of this week's local ballot is seen as an indication of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general election, including whether frustrations with local government failures are changing political loyalties.

About 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters cast ballots, the electoral commission said. Turnout was an estimated 54.5%, up from 46% in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections.

Coalition bargaining

The pro-business, centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) was placing second with just over 24% of votes, according to the 80% count.

This was up from nearly 22% in the 2021 local government election.

The party was set to maintain control of the tourism magnet city of Cape Town and was also leading in the battle for Johannesburg, the country's financial capital where it ran a spirited campaign spearheaded by its former leader Helen Zille.

Former president Jacob Zuma's breakaway opposition uMkhonto weSizwe party (MKP) — contesting local government elections for the first time — was third with just over nine percent.

It was leading in the eastern metropolitan municipality of eThekwini, which includes the port city of Durban, the capital of KwaZulu-Natal province that is Zuma's Zulu homeland.

With outright majorities unlikely to be assured in several major cities, the results will usher in complex coalition negotiations as parties start bargaining to assemble the alliances needed to govern.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now to rise above ... and to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours, and will continue to do so today," he said.

While some of the ANC losses are down to disillusionment after years of corruption and mismanagement, chunks of its support base have also been won over by splinter parties like the MKP in the country's increasingly fragmented political landscape.

"Key among the reasons why the ANC is losing votes is because of the emergence of the parties such as the MKP," said university lecturer and analyst Sanet Solomons.

"The smaller parties have been part of coalitions, but those coalitions have in the past been quite unstable and that is not going to improve service delivery," political science professor Amanda Gouws told AFP.

articles.title: Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability
articles.summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
articles.preview: November 6, 2026 France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have? Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
articles.body:
November 6, 2026

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

A barometer of France's public finances

The spread acts as a kind of fever gauge for bond markets, explains Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide towards a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he explained.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fuelled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE (the French national statistics agency — the ed.), 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

Echoes of the eurozone crisis

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

A warning shot for Germany

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warns the Mannheim-based economist.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left La France insoumise (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire." "Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he claims.

'Fairy tales from the left and the right'

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales." Their common message, he says, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," the expert points out.

"In the past, currency devaluations (of the French franc — the ed.) made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This piece was originally published in German.

The Listening Post

Donald Trump and the Republicans struggle to spin a historic defeat in the US midterms.

It was the most expensive election in American history: nearly $12bn spent, much of it on advertisements, with the majority of that money going to Republican candidates. But most voters weren’t buying it. The result: a Democratic sweep on a scale not seen in half a century.

In the aftermath of the vote, United States President Donald Trump – who has long revelled in his ability to turn controversy and crisis into spectacle – appeared to lose control of the narrative. The scale of the Republican defeat amounts to a repudiation of Trump’s politics and the US-Israel war on Iran. Meenakshi Ravi and Richard Gizbert examine the political and media fallout.

Contributors:

Alex Shephard – Senior editor, The New Republic

Rob Arlett – former Trump state campaign chair & Republican strategist

Maya Berry – Executive director, Arab American Institute

articles.title: Iran's health ministry denies report on iodine distribution over US strike fears
articles.summary: Iran's health ministry denies report on iodine distribution over US strike fears Iran's health ministry has denied a report by The Times of London that it was distributing iodine tablets near its nuclear sites to prepare for possible US strikes. "No Ministry of Health official has spoken to The Times, and the quote attributed to the ministry is false," Hossein Kermanpour, head of the ministry's public relations and information centre, wrote on X . He said the health system was prepared for various scenarios and threats from "an enemy that does not even spare children". But he added that declaring a state of war was not within the ministry's authority. He called publishing unverified reports at such a time "irresponsible". The Times of London had cited an unnamed health ministry official who said Iran was handing out iodine tablets to communities near its nuclear facilities. The official was quoted as saying, “Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime," and that in every war, Iran had tried to distribute the tablets, which help protect the thyroid gland from radiation, within two to three kilometres of its nuclear sites.

Donald Trump, incassata in parte la delusione per la sonora sconfitta subita alle midterm, non cede e torna all'attacco, lanciando un chiaro avvertimento: "Non mi arrenderò mai". Malgrado la pesante batosta, il tycoon ritrova energie e spara ad alzo zero contro i democratici, accusandoli del 'giovedì nero' di Wall Street. E, mentre dietro le quinte si tratta, rispolvera le minacce all'Iran: 'O fanno l'accordo o li distruggo'. Intanto, nell'ambito della resa dei conti apertasi alla Casa Bianca e all'interno del partito repubblicano, cade la prima testa: è quella del capo dello staff del presidente Susie Wiles.

Al suo posto Trump ha nominato Steven Miller, suo fedelissimo e architetto delle politiche trumpiane sull'immigrazione, assecondando così le richieste giunte da una parte dei leader del movimento Maga. Il contraccolpo del voto sui mercati finanziari da al tycoon lo spunto per sferrare il primo vero attacco ai democratici dalle elezioni: è colpa loro se Wall Street ha vissuto quella che definisce "una delle giornate peggiori della sua storia".

Perché lo tsunami blu ha mandato in fumo 3.200 miliardi di dollari di capitalizzazione messi insieme "con un impegno enorme", per colpa - accusa - dei propositi dem di regolamentare Big Tech. Il tycoon, poi, rivendica "al 100%" il pieno supporto alla Super Intelligenza, convinto che "sia miope" non dotarsene, a dispetto della chiara bocciatura dei data center emersa dalle urne in tutto il Paese. Sull'Iran, poi, il tycoon appare indeciso, ma torna a usare parole dure: "Vogliamo andare oltre e limitarci a certificare l'accordo, il che significherebbe che una cosa del genere non accadrà mai più...Oppure possiamo distruggere il resto del Paese, ma preferirei non farlo, se possibile. Ma forse sarò costretto, lo saprete presto".

Nel frattempo ha riunito per la prima volta nel dopo midterm i consiglieri per la sicurezza nazionale. Mentre i media americani hanno dato conto del pressing del vicepresidente Jd Vance per una soluzione negoziale con Teheran, il primo punto del suo programma di rifondazione della destra Usa in vista delle presidenziali del 2028. Secondo Axios, il presidente, almeno per ora, valuta tre opzioni: lanciare nuovi attacchi (secondo Fox News il 9 novembre, con la luna nuova), continuare a strangolare economicamente il regime iraniano o raggiungere un accordo che includa significative concessioni a favore di Teheran. Il tutto nel mezzo dell'intensa attività diplomatica, incluse le numerose telefonate tra il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi e i mediatori regionali di Qatar, Arabia Saudita, Turchia, Emirati Arabi Uniti, Oman ed Egitto. Poi c'è la resa di conti nel partito. Il tracollo elettorale repubblicano ha aperto la battaglia per le primarie del Grand Old Party con vista sul 2028: Vance è finito sotto accusa per aver attribuito il disastro delle urne alla guerra in Iran, dimenticandosi "dei dazi e del costo della vita" (ha rilevato il Wall Street Journal), e altri esponenti di spicco del partito sembrano voler prendere le distanze dall'amministrazione, definendo le proprie posizioni.

Si è già creato, in altri termini, un ampio margine di manovra per gli aspiranti candidati alla Casa Bianca, tra cui il governatore della Florida Ron DeSantis e il senatore del Texas Ted Cruz, per contrapporsi a Vance. Mentre il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio, a dispetto della smentita sulla sua uscita dall'amministrazione Trump per la corsa del 2028, appare in condizioni leggermente migliori su Vance: ma il peso negativo del voto di martedì potrebbe essere per entrambi un peso insormontabile, dato che le elezioni hanno rappresentato un vero e proprio referendum sul loro operato. Trump intanto, incassando i dati più che positivi sull'occupazione di ottobre, continua a raccogliere fondi per le sue attività politiche con un obiettivo ben preciso: Axios - secondo cui il tycoon continua ad alimentare i suoi Super Pac, come Maga Inc - ha riferito che The Donald punta ad avere la forza per influenzare gli scenari del 2028, mettendo sotto pressione i repubblicani che vorrebbero rompere con lui. Infine, la posizione del capo del Pentagono Pete Hegseth appare sempre più complicata: il deputato repubblicano Thomas Massie, deciso oppositore di Trump, presenterà la prossima settimana, alla ripresa dei lavori del Congresso, la mozione di impeachment contro il segretario alla Difesa. "C'è un solo scenario in cui non la ripresenterò: se Hegseth si dimette", ha scritto Massie in un post su X.

Police surrounded the protesters before the mayor ordered the demonstration to end. Riot officers subsequently intervened, with several arrests reported. The protest was organised by Dutch activist collective Geef Tegengas, alongside a separate mobilisation by environmental campaign group Fossielvrij NL. Campaigners oppose the development over its expected electricity consumption, its impact on housing plans and concerns about Microsoft's activities. The project, developed by Pure Data Centres for Microsoft, involves three towers approximately 85 metres high, with an investment exceeding $1 billion. Protesters argue that the facilities could consume as much electricity as all Amsterdam households combined, a claim that has not been independently established. The action formed part of an international campaign against large-scale data centres, with demonstrations planned across several European countries. Both Pure Data Centres and Microsoft said they respected peaceful protest, while urging demonstrators to avoid unlawful actions.

articles.title: I pm possono procedere su Giusi Bartolozzi per false dichiarazioni
articles.summary: Sentenza della Consulta: 'Devono comunicarlo alla Camera'. Possibile sollevare un altro conflitto
articles.preview: La Consulta accoglie parzialmente il ricorso della Camera nei confronti del Tribunale dei ministri e della Procura di Roma sulla posizione di Giusi Bartolozzi. Ma per l'ex capo di gabinetto del ministero della Giustizia al momento il bicchiere è mezzo vuoto: secondo la Corte costituzionale, i magistrati di piazzale Clodio possono procedere, ma dovranno prima informare la Camera, in merito alle indagini che vedono la ex dirigente di via Arenula accusata di false dichiarazioni al pm sul caso del generale libico Almasri, che fu arrestato a Torino e poi…
articles.body:
La Consulta accoglie parzialmente il ricorso della Camera nei confronti del Tribunale dei ministri e della Procura di Roma sulla posizione di Giusi Bartolozzi. Ma per l'ex capo di gabinetto del ministero della Giustizia al momento il bicchiere è mezzo vuoto: secondo la Corte costituzionale, i magistrati di piazzale Clodio possono procedere, ma dovranno prima informare la Camera, in merito alle indagini che vedono la ex dirigente di via Arenula accusata di false dichiarazioni al pm sul caso del generale libico Almasri, che fu arrestato a Torino e poi rilasciato e riportato con un aereo dei servizi a Tripoli.

Ma la questione giuridica, che va avanti a colpi di istanze, non sembra affatto conclusa: l'obbligo per la Procura di dare comunicazione alla Camera sull'indagine nei confronti di Bartolozzi potrebbe aprire ad un nuovo ricorso alla Consulta, visto che l'assemblea dei deputati a questo punto ha la facoltà di sollevare l'ennesimo conflitto di attribuzione di fronte ai giudici della Corte. E la sentenza della Corte, di fatto interlocutoria, disegna uno scenario ancora incerto, che non si esaurisce solo all'indagine per l'accusa di false dichiarazioni. Oltre a questo reato, 'connesso' a quelli di cui era accusato il Guardasigilli Carlo Nordio, resta la questione sui presunti reati 'in concorso' con il ministro, per i quali è stata invece negata l'autorizzazione a procedere assieme ad altri vertici del governo (nello specifico, omissione di atti d'ufficio e concorso in favoreggiamento personale aggravato).

La Camera dei deputati aveva fatto ricorso contro i magistrati romani proprio perché avrebbero dovuto chiedere anche per Bartolozzi l'autorizzazione a procedere, per il ruolo da lei rivestito all'epoca al ministero. Con la sentenza di oggi la Consulta risponde che, laddove avesse configurato un tale 'concorso', il Tribunale avrebbe dovuto in quel caso chiedere alla Camera l'autorizzazione a procedere anche nei confronti della stessa Bartolozzi, oltre che del ministro. La Corte ha infatti rilevato che, "all'esito delle indagini svolte dal Tribunale nei confronti del ministro, la Procura aveva espressamente invitato il Tribunale a qualificare la condotta di Bartolozzi come concorso nei reati ascritti al ministro Nordio, o, alternativamente, a ipotizzare a suo carico il reato di false dichiarazioni durante le indagini. In virtù del principio di leale collaborazione tra i poteri dello Stato, a fronte di questa sollecitazione, il Tribunale avrebbe dovuto esplicitare le ragioni per le quali non ha ritenuto di configurare, in capo a Bartolozzi, una possibile responsabilità per concorso nei reati attribuiti al ministro".

Sul reato di false dichiarazioni al pm di cui Bartolozzi è accusata, restano poi da sciogliere dei nodi. Se i magistrati procedono per un altro reato, potevano sentire la ex capo di gabinetto solo come 'persona informata sui fatti' e quindi senza un avvocato? Da questo punto di vista c'è chi non esclude al momento anche un ricorso per la lesione dei diritti di difesa di Bartolozzi. E per la ex dirigente di via Arenula, alle beghe giudiziarie personali, in queste stesse ore si aggiungono anche quelle legate a suo marito Gaetano Armao, ex vicepresidente della Regione Sicilia, accusato di corruzione in tutt'altra vicenda: per lui il Gip di Palermo ha disposto gli arresti domiciliari sul caso delle autorizzazioni ambientali della regione.

articles.title: UN says struggling to help millions fleeing Sudan war find shelter
articles.summary: The United Nations on Friday said about 15.4 million people who have fled conflict in Sudan need emergency shelter and essential household items, but humanitarian organisations are facing funding shortages.
articles.preview: Sudan Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday. After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items. But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages. And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.
articles.body:
Sudan

Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday.

After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items.

But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages.

And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.

The war raging since April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the regular army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within the country, millions have fled across borders and millions more have returned home — often finding houses, infrastructure and essential services damaged or destroyed.

Since the start of the year, Refaat said the UN agency had distributed more than 40,000 tents.

"But our warehouses are completely empty now," he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Khartoum.

"We could soon reach a point where families desperately need shelter but there is simply nothing left."

In a joint statement, UNHCR and IOM said for those returning home getting help to find shelter "is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives".

But only one third of the $179 million needed this year to provide shelter has so far been funded, Abubakarr Jalloh, UNHCR's deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high,” the UNHCR official said.

“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Jalloh stressed.

The agencies said less than half of the $2.9 billion needed for the overall humanitarian aid plan for Sudan had been funded.

Nella regione di Kiev si registrano tre feriti a seguito di un attacco notturno delle truppe russe. Un incendio è scoppiato in un edificio residenziale privato e in una dependance nel quartiere di Boryspil. Entrambi gli edifici sono stati completamente distrutti. Tre persone sono rimaste ferite. Lo ha riferito il capo dell'amministrazione militare regionale di Kiev, Timur Tkachenko

A quanto riporta il funzionario, "le infrastrutture energetiche dei distretti di Bila Tserkva e Obukhiv sono state danneggiate a seguito dell'attacco nemico. Anche nel distretto di Obukhiv, l'onda d'urto ha danneggiato le finestre dell'edificio scolastico e del dormitorio di un istituto di istruzione. I servizi di emergenza sono al lavoro sul posto.

I russi inoltre hanno attaccato un impianto infrastrutturale energetico nella regione di Mykolaiv. Mosca ha inoltre preso di mira con un drone Fpv e un Uav Molniya nella località di Kutsurubsk, nel distretto di Mykolaiv, un edificio annesso al villaggio di Dmytrivka che è stato danneggiato. In entrambi i casi non si sono registrate vittime.

Un uomo è stato ucciso in un attacco stamattina da parte dei russi nel distretto di Sarny, nella regione di Rivne. Lo ha riferito il capo dell'amministrazione militare regionale, Oleksandr Koval, su Telegram. Secondo i dati preliminari, anche una casa e un camion sono stati danneggiati dall'attacco.

Kallas: 'Non ci può essere nessun accordo sull'Ucraina senza l'Europa'

"Qualsiasi accordo deve poi essere attuato e per l'attuazione è necessario il coinvolgimento dell'Europa e se non ne siamo parte, non lo attueremo". Lo ha detto l'alto rappresentante Ue Kaja Kallas a proposito di possibili intese fra Russia e Usa sulla testa dell'Ucraina e dell'Europa. "Abbiamo già assistito a dei tentativi in tal senso, se si pensa all'accordo o all'intesa di Anchorage. Ma poi non ha funzionato semplicemente perché l'Europa non ha dato il proprio sostegno", ha notato. "Noi dobbiamo essere parte di queste discussioni".

Kiev: 'A Komyshuvakha bilancio sale a 53 morti, circa 50 dispersi'

Sono in corso le operazioni di ricerca sul luogo del raid aereo del 2 novembre nel villaggio di Komyshuvakha, nella regione di Zaporizhzia. Al momento si sa che sono stati recuperati i corpi di 53 persone, mentre un'altra cinquantina di persone risultano disperse. Lo ha reso noto Yulia Barysheva, portavoce della Direzione Generale del Servizio Statale di Emergenza dell'Ucraina nella regione di Zaporizhzhia, durante una conferenza stampa interministeriale, secondo quanto riportato da un corrispondente di Ukrinform.

Le autorità russe, 'droni ucraini causano incendio in un'area industriale a Krasnodar'

Il centro per la risposta alle emergenze del Territorio di Krasnodar, nella Russia meridionale, ha segnalato che un incendio è scoppiato in una delle aziende del centro abitato di Afipsky a causa della caduta di rottami di un drone ucraino. Le autorità non hanno specificato quale struttura sia stata danneggiata, ma secondo le analisi di informazioni aperte del canale Telegram Astra, l'incendio si sarebbe verificato nella raffineria di Afipsky, con una capacità produttiva di 9,1 milioni di tonnellate di petrolio all'anno. Secondo le testimonianze di residenti del luogo il fumo ha avvolto l'area intorno alla raffineria e la colonna di fumo ha raggiunto il capoluogo, Krasnodar, che dista circa 20 chilometri.

articles.summary: Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.

Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.
articles.body:
Water

Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.

According to a new report from the UN Children's Agency, attacks that damaged or destroyed water and sanitation systems in conflict rose threefold between 2021 and 2025.

That deprives children of safe drinking water and exposes them to disease from poor sanitation. The report also documents how children in Gaza have been killed or injured while queuing for water.

Longer more dangerous journeys also raise their risk of sexual violence and take time away from school.

Efforts need to be made to guarantee humanitarian access so that water and energy supplies keep running, UNICEF says.

It also calls for the protection of those who operate and maintain water systems and for all attacks to be systematically documented.

articles.body:
Czech arms makers look spaceward in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven boom

November 6, 2026

Czech arms makers have thrived on demand linked to the war in Ukraine. To sustain their growth, they need to look beyond ammunition and toward new technologies — and even space.

The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.

This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.

From 90s startup to major European player

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.

It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.

The impact of the war in Ukraine

The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.

In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.

By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.

Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.

Historical link

"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.

Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.

At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

Export dependence

However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.

As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."

What the future holds

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."

Space mission

CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.

The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.

Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.

"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

articles.title: For people in Iran, a constant threat of war and dearth of information
articles.summary: Most people in Iran have little idea of the course of the US-led war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, the population must navigate conflicting rumors and fears of a nuclear attack.
